blocks.text: So much for Noah's raven according to the Hebrews. The Greeks, however, say something very different: their version apparently denies the very thing that Moses explicitly asserts, namely that the raven came back. For it reads Ἐξελθὼν οὐκ ἀνέστρεψεν [exelthōn ouk anestrepsen], Having gone out (from the ark, the raven) did not return, for the Hebrew ויצא יצוא ושוב, And it went out going out, and returning. The Syriac likewise has ܘܢܦܩ ܡܦܩ ܘܠܐ ܗܦܟ, And it went out going out, and did not return. And Jerome: Which went out, and did not return. And two Arabic manuscripts that I saw in Sweden have لم يعون [lam yaʿūn] did not return, or فلم يعد [fa-lam yaʿud] and did not return. But the former is plainly rendered from the Greek version, the latter from the Syriac. The ancient doctors follow this same reading: Hilary, Arnobius and Pseudo-Jerome on Psalm 146; the genuine Jerome in the Dialogue against the Luciferians, chapter 8; Ambrose, On Noah and the Ark, chapter 17; Sulpicius Severus, History, book 1; Augustine on Genesis, book 1, Question 13, and elsewhere; Chrysostom on Genesis, book 2. Also Eutychius of Alexandria, p. 40: فذهب الغراب ولم يرجع [fa-dhahaba al-ghurāb wa-lam yarjiʿ] And the raven went away, and did not return. In short, all the ancients I have been able to come across, except Procopius alone, who does not admit the negation. Hence a twofold question arises: first, where this difference of readings came from; [II, 802] second, which reading is true and to be preferred to the other. To the first, many answer that the Hebrews and the Greeks can very well be reconciled, since both statements are truly made, that the raven returned and that it did not return: it returned to the ark, or onto the ark, but did not return into the ark. This answer is empty. Neither reading says that the raven returned, or did not return, into the ark or onto the ark; rather, one of them says simply that the raven returned, the other that it did not return, and these are flatly contrary. If someone rendered the words of Moses in Gen. XXII, 1. God tested Abraham as God did not test Abraham, would he not be a false translator, even though it is true in a certain sense that God did not test Abraham, namely in the sense in which James ^{a)} said that God tempts no one? Moreover, although the Hebrew text does not say explicitly that the raven returned into the ark, this is plainly implied. For the words run: It went out going out, and returning, until, etc. That is, it often went out and often returned. And to go out of the ark often, it had to go back into it often, since no one goes out of a house who has not gone into it. According to others, the Hebrew שוב [col. 211] means not only to return but also to recede: as in verse 3 of this very chapter, וישבו המים מעל הארץ הלוך ושוב, And the waters returned from the face of the earth, going and returning, that is, they receded steadily. In the same way, they say, the raven went out going out from the ark, ושוב, and returning, that is, receding. And to recede from the ark, they assert, is the same as not to return to it. But neither is this answer adequate. For whatever they say, שוב properly means to return. Even when the waters are said to have returned from the face of the earth, they are said to have returned because they had previously submerged it, and were going from the face of the earth back to their natural place, that is, into the sea, etc. Moreover, שוב is not taken in the sense of receding unless the particle מן, that is, from or out of, is added, which nowhere appears here. Finally, these words do not hang together: The raven went out, going out and receding, until the waters had dried up. For the raven went out on the eleventh day of the eleventh month, Gen. VIII, 5. 6. And the waters finally dried up at the beginning of the following year, Gen. VIII, 13., that is, fifty days after the raven went out. No one would say that the raven was receding from the ark during that whole time. But granting, without conceding, that the Hebrew words can be rendered The raven went out, going out and receding, the Greek version, The raven, having gone out, did not return, would still be very different from them. For to go away and recede from somewhere over a journey of fifty days is not the same as to go away from there and not return before the fiftieth day. Others hold that the Jews removed the negation from the Hebrew text; they are refuted by the agreement of the Samaritan codex with the Hebrew. Besides, the two Chaldees, Jonathan and Onkelos, have here ונפק מפק ותאיב. And the Samaritan translator: ࠅࠍࠐࠒ ࠌࠐࠅࠒ ࠅࠕࠁ And it went out going out and returning. And the Arabic edited at Paris: فجعل [fa-jaʿala] [II, 803] فخرج يخرج ويرجع [fa-kharaja yakhruju wa-yarjiʿu] And it went out, and came back. And Erpenianus: وخرج خارجا وراجعا [wa-kharaja khārijan wa-rājiʿan] And it went out going out, and returning. Josephus too, Antiq. book 1, ch. 4: πρὸς Νῶχον ἐπανῆλθε [pros Nōchon epanēlthe], It returned to Noah. Moreover, in Bereshit Rabbah and in the Aggadah, which are among the oldest books of the Hebrews, this passage reads exactly as in our codices. Finally, I am fully convinced that Jerome read it this way too, and that the text of the Hebrew Questions is corrupt where it reads: „And concerning the raven it is said otherwise (in the Hebrew text): And he sent out the raven, and it went out going and not returning“. For one should read going and returning. If you read and not returning, why would he assert that it is said otherwise in the Hebrew text than in the Greek? This observation of the bishop of Chisamus is entirely correct. Nor did the Jews have any reason to corrupt that passage, since it matters nothing to them whether the raven is believed to have returned or not. Lastly, there are those who think that the negation was inserted into the Greek codices, either deliberately or through the carelessness of scribes. Neither is at all likely. Not the first: just as the rest of the Hebrews had no reason to remove the negation from the Hebrew text, so the Greek translators had no reason to add it to their version. Nor the second: if you remove the negation from the Greek words (Ἐξελθὼν οὐκ ἀνέστρεψεν, ἕως τοῦ ξηρανθῆναι τὸ ὕδωρ [exelthōn ouk anestrepsen, heōs tou xēranthēnai to hydōr], Having gone out it did not return, until the waters had dried up), the whole structure of the sentence falls apart, and the result will make no sense: Having gone out it returned, until the waters had dried up. Since, therefore, this version is framed in words from which the negation can in no way be absent, it is clear that it was written by the translators themselves, and not slipped in and inserted into the text by a scribal error.
